# tooltip.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joncoronel/cubby-ui/blob/main/content/docs/components/(primitives)/tooltip.mdx

title: Tooltip
description: Contextual information that appears on hover or focus
type: primitive

import {
  Tooltip,
  TooltipContent,
  TooltipTrigger,
} from "@/registry/default/tooltip/tooltip";

A tooltip shows a short, non-interactive label on hover or focus. Use it to name icon-only buttons or add a brief hint; for anything clickable or longer than a phrase, use [`Popover`](/docs/components/popover) instead.

## Preview

<ComponentPreview component="tooltip" example="tooltip-basic" />

## Installation

<ComponentInstall component="tooltip" />

## Usage

<ComponentUsage component="tooltip" />

## Composition

```text
Tooltip
├── TooltipTrigger
└── TooltipContent
```

`TooltipContent` composes the portal, positioner, popup, and optional arrow internally, so you pass your label directly inside it. Wrap your app in `TooltipProvider` to share open and close timing across tooltips.

## Examples

### Detached Trigger

Use `createTooltipHandle()` to link a trigger outside the `Tooltip` component.

<ComponentPreview component="tooltip" example="tooltip-detached-trigger" />

### Controlled

Control the tooltip's open state externally using the `open` and `onOpenChange` props.

<ComponentPreview component="tooltip" example="tooltip-controlled" />

### Animated Transitions

Animate the tooltip when switching between multiple triggers with different payloads.

<ComponentPreview component="tooltip" example="tooltip-animated" />

## Accessibility

### Don't rely on the tooltip as the only label

A tooltip only appears on hover or focus, so it can't be the sole accessible name for an icon-only control. Give the trigger its own text (a visually hidden span or `aria-label`) and use the tooltip for the same or supplementary hint.

```tsx showLineNumbers
<TooltipTrigger render={<Button variant="outline" size="icon" />}>
  <PlusIcon />
  <span className="sr-only">Add to library</span>
</TooltipTrigger>
<TooltipContent>Add to library</TooltipContent>
```

## API Reference

The Tooltip component is built on top of [Base UI's Tooltip](https://base-ui.com/react/components/tooltip). All Base UI props are supported. The documentation below only covers custom props and modified defaults specific to our implementation.

For the complete Base UI API, see the [Base UI Tooltip documentation](https://base-ui.com/react/components/tooltip).

### Utilities

#### createTooltipHandle

Creates a handle that connects a tooltip to one or more external `TooltipTrigger` components. Useful when the triggers need to live outside the `Tooltip`, for example when each row in a list has its own trigger but they all share one tooltip.

```tsx
import { createTooltipHandle } from "@/registry/default/tooltip/tooltip";

const handle = createTooltipHandle();
```

##### Passing data from the trigger to the tooltip

The handle accepts an optional `<Payload>` generic that types a value each trigger can pass along. The tooltip reads it through a render-prop child, so you can render different content per trigger without duplicating the tooltip markup.

```tsx
type User = { id: string; name: string };

const handle = createTooltipHandle<User>();

// Multiple triggers, each with its own payload:
users.map((user) => (
  <TooltipTrigger key={user.id} handle={handle} payload={user}>
    {user.name}
  </TooltipTrigger>
));

// One shared tooltip that renders based on the active trigger:
<Tooltip handle={handle}>
  <TooltipContent>
    {({ payload: user }) => <p>{user?.name}</p>}
  </TooltipContent>
</Tooltip>;
```

Without the `<User>` generic, `payload` inside the render prop resolves to `unknown`.

### Props

#### TooltipContent

Composed component for common tooltip layouts. Combines `Tooltip.Portal`, `Tooltip.Positioner`, and `Tooltip.Popup`. Optionally renders `Tooltip.Arrow`. Props are forwarded to the Positioner and Popup components.

<ApiProp name="arrow" fullType="boolean" defaultValue="false">
  Show or hide the tooltip arrow pointing to the trigger. Custom prop not
  available in Base UI.

<ApiProp
  name="side"
  fullType="'top' | 'right' | 'bottom' | 'left' | 'inline-start' | 'inline-end'"
  defaultValue='"top"'
>
  Which side of the trigger to position the tooltip. Flattened from Positioner.

<ApiProp
  name="align"
  fullType="'start' | 'center' | 'end'"
  defaultValue='"center"'
>
  How to align the tooltip relative to the trigger. Flattened from Positioner.

<ApiProp name="sideOffset" fullType="number" defaultValue="8">
  Distance in pixels between trigger and tooltip. Flattened from Positioner.
  Base UI defaults to `0`.

<ApiProp name="alignOffset" fullType="number" defaultValue="0">
  Offset along the alignment axis. Flattened from Positioner.

<ApiProp
  name="collisionBoundary"
  fullType="Element | Element[] | 'clipping-ancestors'"
>
  Boundary for collision detection. Flattened from Positioner.

<ApiProp
  name="collisionPadding"
  fullType="number | Partial<Record<Side, number>>"
  defaultValue="10"
>
  Padding from collision boundary. Flattened from Positioner. Base UI defaults
  to `5`.

<ApiProp name="sticky" fullType="boolean" defaultValue="false">
  Whether to keep the tooltip visible in the viewport after the anchor element
  has scrolled out of view. Flattened from Positioner.

<ApiProp
  name="positionMethod"
  fullType="'absolute' | 'fixed'"
  defaultValue='"absolute"'
>
  CSS position method. Flattened from Positioner.

<ApiProp name="arrowPadding" fullType="number">
  Minimum padding between arrow and tooltip edges. Flattened from Positioner.
  Base UI defaults to `5`.

<ApiProp name="container" fullType="HTMLElement | undefined">
  Portal container element. Flattened from Portal.

<ApiProp name="level" fullType="1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8" defaultValue="2">
  Surface elevation level. Tooltip defaults to `2` (lightest tier), quieter than popovers and dropdowns. See the [Surfaces](/docs/getting-started/surfaces) docs.

<ApiProp name="shadowLevel" fullType="1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8" defaultValue="2">
  Shadow weight. Defaults to `2` to match the lightweight visual of tooltips.

### Modified Defaults

Our implementation changes the following Base UI prop defaults:

- **TooltipContent**: `sideOffset` defaults to `8` (Base UI defaults to `0`)
- **TooltipContent**: `collisionPadding` defaults to `10` (Base UI defaults to `5`)

---

# forms.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joncoronel/cubby-ui/blob/main/content/docs/getting-started/forms.mdx

title: Forms
description: A guide to building forms with Cubby UI components

## Overview

Cubby UI provides three components for building accessible forms: [Form](/docs/components/form), [Field](/docs/components/field), and [Fieldset](/docs/components/fieldset). These wrap Base UI's form primitives, providing native constraint validation, custom validation, accessible labeling, error display, and integration with third-party libraries.

## Quick start

```tsx
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/cubby-ui/button";
import { Field, FieldControl, FieldError, FieldLabel } from "@/components/ui/cubby-ui/field";
import { Form } from "@/components/ui/cubby-ui/form";

<Form onFormSubmit={(values) => console.log(values)}>
  <Field name="email">
    <FieldLabel>Email</FieldLabel>
    <FieldControl type="email" required />
    <FieldError match="valueMissing">Email is required</FieldError>
    <FieldError match="typeMismatch">Enter a valid email</FieldError>
  </Field>
  <Button type="submit">Submit</Button>
</Form>
```

## Labeling form controls

Every form control needs an accessible label. The correct label component depends on the control type.

### Input-type controls

Use `FieldLabel` to label these controls:

- [Input](/docs/components/input)
- [Number Field](/docs/components/number-field)
- [Combobox](/docs/components/combobox) (when the input is outside the popup)
- [Checkbox](/docs/components/checkbox)
- [Radio](/docs/components/radio-group)
- [Switch](/docs/components/switch)

For Checkbox, Radio, and Switch, wrap the control inside `FieldLabel` for implicit labeling:

```tsx
<Field name="terms">
  <FieldLabel>
    <Checkbox required />
    I accept the terms
  </FieldLabel>
</Field>
```

### Trigger-based controls

These controls have their own label component. Do **not** use `FieldLabel` for them:

- [Select](/docs/components/select): use `SelectLabel`
- [Slider](/docs/components/slider): use `SliderLabel`

```tsx
<Field name="country">
  <Select items={countries} required>
    <SelectLabel>Country</SelectLabel>
    <SelectTrigger>
      <SelectValue placeholder="Select a country" />
    </SelectTrigger>
    <SelectContent>...</SelectContent>
  </Select>
  <FieldError />
</Field>
```

### Descriptions

`FieldDescription` adds accessible helper text to any field, regardless of control type:

```tsx
<Field name="timezone">
  <Select items={timezones}>
    <SelectLabel>Time zone</SelectLabel>
    <SelectTrigger>...</SelectTrigger>
    <SelectContent>...</SelectContent>
  </Select>
  <FieldDescription>Used for notifications and reminders</FieldDescription>
</Field>
```

## Grouping controls with Fieldset

Use `Fieldset` with `FieldsetLegend` when a single label applies to multiple controls, such as radio groups, checkbox groups, or multi-thumb sliders. Compose with the `render` prop to merge the fieldset element with a group component:

```tsx
<Field name="role">
  <Fieldset render={<RadioGroup defaultValue="member" />}>
    <FieldsetLegend>Role</FieldsetLegend>
    <FieldItem>
      <FieldLabel>
        <RadioGroupItem value="member" />
        Member
      </FieldLabel>
    </FieldItem>
    <FieldItem>
      <FieldLabel>
        <RadioGroupItem value="admin" />
        Admin
      </FieldLabel>
    </FieldItem>
  </Fieldset>
</Field>
```

Use `FieldItem` to wrap each individual option so it gets its own label and description.

## Validation

### Constraint validation

Use native HTML attributes on `FieldControl` (`required`, `pattern`, `minLength`, `type`, `min`, `max`, etc.) and `FieldError` to display the browser's native error message:

```tsx
<Field name="website">
  <FieldLabel>Website</FieldLabel>
  <FieldControl type="url" required pattern="https?://.*" />
  <FieldError />
</Field>
```

### Per-state custom messages

To override native messages (for i18n or branding), use multiple `FieldError` components with the `match` prop. Each one renders only for the specified validity state:

```tsx
<Field name="password">
  <FieldLabel>Password</FieldLabel>
  <FieldControl type="password" required minLength={8} />
  <FieldError match="valueMissing">Password is required</FieldError>
  <FieldError match="tooShort">Must be at least 8 characters</FieldError>
</Field>
```

Available `match` values: `valueMissing`, `typeMismatch`, `patternMismatch`, `tooShort`, `tooLong`, `rangeUnderflow`, `rangeOverflow`, `stepMismatch`, `badInput`, `customError`.

### Custom validation

Use the `validate` prop on `Field` for custom logic. Supports async functions:

```tsx
<Field
  name="username"
  validationMode="onChange"
  validationDebounceTime={300}
  validate={async (value) => {
    const taken = await checkUsername(value);
    return taken ? "Username is taken" : null;
  }}
>
  <FieldLabel>Username</FieldLabel>
  <FieldControl />
  <FieldError />
</Field>
```

### Server-side validation

Pass errors from your server to `Form`'s `errors` prop. Keys match field `name` attributes:

```tsx
const [errors, setErrors] = React.useState({});

<Form
  errors={errors}
  onSubmit={async (event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    const response = await submitToServer(new FormData(event.currentTarget));
    if (response.errors) setErrors(response.errors);
  }}
>
  <Field name="email">...</Field>
</Form>
```

## Submitting data

### Native onSubmit

Use `onSubmit` with `FormData` for standard form submission:

```tsx
<Form onSubmit={(event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const formData = new FormData(event.currentTarget);
  // send formData
}} />
```

### JavaScript object with onFormSubmit

Use `onFormSubmit` to receive values as a plain object. `preventDefault` is called automatically:

```tsx
<Form onFormSubmit={(values) => {
  // values is { name: "...", email: "...", ... }
}} />
```

## Third-party library integration

### React Hook Form

Use `Controller` to bridge RHF state with Field's `invalid`, `dirty`, and `touched` props. Use `onValueChange` on `FieldControl` (not `onChange`) and `match={!!error}` on `FieldError`:

```tsx
<Controller
  name="username"
  control={control}
  rules={{
    required: "This is a required field.",
    minLength: { value: 3, message: "At least 3 characters." },
  }}
  render={({
    field: { ref, name, value, onBlur, onChange },
    fieldState: { invalid, isTouched, isDirty, error },
  }) => (
    <Field name={name} invalid={invalid} touched={isTouched} dirty={isDirty}>
      <FieldLabel>Username</FieldLabel>
      <FieldControl
        ref={ref}
        value={value}
        onBlur={onBlur}
        onValueChange={onChange}
        placeholder="e.g. alice132"
      />
      <FieldError match={!!error}>{error?.message}</FieldError>
    </Field>
  )}
/>
```

For RHF to focus invalid fields, forward `ref` to the underlying control - typically via `inputRef` on wrapper components (Select, Switch, Checkbox, RadioGroup) or directly as `ref` on input-like components.

### TanStack Form

Use `form.Field` (TanStack's field) to manage state, and `Field` (Cubby UI) for the UI. Note: the Base UI `Form` component isn't needed with TanStack Form - use a native `<form>` element instead.

```tsx
import { useForm, revalidateLogic } from "@tanstack/react-form";

const form = useForm({
  defaultValues: { email: "" },
  onSubmit: ({ value }) => {
    // submit value
  },
  validationLogic: revalidateLogic({
    mode: "submit",
    modeAfterSubmission: "change",
  }),
  validators: {
    onDynamic: ({ value }) => {
      const errors: Record<string, string> = {};
      if (!value.email) errors.email = "Email is required";
      return Object.keys(errors).length === 0
        ? undefined
        : { form: errors, fields: errors };
    },
  },
});

<form
  onSubmit={(event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    form.handleSubmit();
  }}
  noValidate
>
  <form.Field name="email">
    {(field) => (
      <Field
        name={field.name}
        invalid={!field.state.meta.isValid}
        dirty={field.state.meta.isDirty}
        touched={field.state.meta.isTouched}
      >
        <FieldLabel>Email</FieldLabel>
        <FieldControl
          value={field.state.value}
          onValueChange={field.handleChange}
          onBlur={field.handleBlur}
        />
        <FieldError match={!field.state.meta.isValid}>
          {field.state.meta.errors.join(",")}
        </FieldError>
      </Field>
    )}
  </form.Field>
</form>
```

## Forms on elevated surfaces

When a form lives inside a Card, Dialog, Sheet, Drawer, or any other elevated container, the form-field defaults will collapse into the parent's white background in light mode. Switch every field that takes a `variant` prop to `variant="elevated"`:

```tsx
<Dialog>
  <DialogContent>
    <Field name="email">
      <FieldLabel>Email</FieldLabel>
      <FieldControl render={<Input variant="elevated" />} type="email" required />
    </Field>
    <Checkbox variant="elevated" />
  </DialogContent>
</Dialog>
```

Applies to Input, Textarea, NumberFieldGroup (not NumberFieldInput), InputGroup, InputOTPSlot, OTPFieldInput, ComboboxInput, ComboboxChips, AutocompleteInput, Checkbox, and RadioGroupItem. Switch handles this automatically; no variant prop needed. See the [Surfaces](/docs/getting-started/surfaces) docs for the full reasoning.

## Component reference

| Component | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| [Form](/docs/components/form) | Form wrapper with `errors`, `onFormSubmit`, `validationMode` |
| [Field](/docs/components/field) | Field wrapper with label, control, description, error, validation |
| [Fieldset](/docs/components/fieldset) | Grouping related fields with a shared legend |

---

# installation.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joncoronel/cubby-ui/blob/main/content/docs/getting-started/installation.mdx

title: Installation
description: How to install and configure Cubby UI in your project

Cubby UI uses the [shadcn CLI](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/cli) to add components to your project. Components are copied directly into your codebase, giving you full ownership and control.

## Prerequisites

Before installing components, ensure your project has:

- **React 19** or later
- **Tailwind CSS 4** configured
- **TypeScript**

## Quick Start

Cubby UI is listed in the official [shadcn registry directory](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/directory), so the `@cubby-ui` namespace resolves automatically. There's no need to add it to your `components.json`.

### 1. Install Base UI

Cubby UI components are built on [Base UI](https://base-ui.com), a headless component library:

<PackageManagerCommand command="@base-ui/react" type="add" />

### 2. Add the theme

Cubby UI ships its theme as a standalone style (`@cubby-ui/style`) covering colors, status colors, radius, easings, and the surface elevation system. Choose the path that matches your project:

<Tabs defaultValue="new">

<TabsList>
  <TabsTrigger value="new">New project</TabsTrigger>
  <TabsTrigger value="existing">Existing project</TabsTrigger>
</TabsList>

<TabsPanels>
<TabsContent value="new">

Scaffold shadcn and install Cubby UI's theme as your project's base in a single command:

<PackageManagerCommand command="shadcn@latest init @cubby-ui/style" />

This creates your `components.json` and writes the full theme into `globals.css`.

</TabsContent>
<TabsContent value="existing">

Already have a shadcn project? Add the theme to it:

<PackageManagerCommand command="shadcn@latest add @cubby-ui/style" />

</TabsContent>
</TabsPanels>
</Tabs>

### 3. Add the root class

Add a `root` class to your application wrapper. This creates a stacking context required by Base UI's portal-based components:

```tsx title="app/layout.tsx"
export default function RootLayout({
  children,
}: {
  children: React.ReactNode;
}) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <div className="root">{children}</div>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

### 4. Add components

Now you can add any Cubby UI component:

<PackageManagerCommand command="shadcn@latest add @cubby-ui/button" />

This will:

- Copy the component source code to your project
- Install any required dependencies
- Set up the necessary utility functions

## Adding Multiple Components

Add multiple components in a single command:

<PackageManagerCommand command="shadcn@latest add @cubby-ui/button @cubby-ui/input @cubby-ui/card" />

Or install all components at once:

<PackageManagerCommand command="shadcn@latest add @cubby-ui/all" />

## What's Included in the Theme

The `@cubby-ui/style` theme adds CSS variables for colors (including status colors), border radius variants, easing functions, the surface elevation system, and Base UI layout requirements. See [Theming](/docs/getting-started/theming) for full details.

## Project Structure

After adding components, your project structure will look like this:

```
components/
  ui/
    cubby-ui/
      button.tsx
      input.tsx
      card.tsx
hooks/
  cubby-ui/
    use-mobile.ts
lib/
  cubby-ui/
    utils.ts
components.json
```

The exact paths depend on your `components.json` configuration.

## Manual Installation

If you prefer not to use the CLI, you can manually copy component source code from the documentation and install dependencies yourself. Each component's documentation page includes the full source code and dependency list.

For the theme setup, copy the CSS variables from the [Theming](/docs/getting-started/theming) guide into your `globals.css`.

## Next Steps

- Browse the [Components](/docs/components) to see what's available
- Learn about [Theming](/docs/getting-started/theming) to customize the look and feel
- Check out individual component pages for usage examples

---

# introduction.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joncoronel/cubby-ui/blob/main/content/docs/getting-started/introduction.mdx

title: Introduction
description: Cubby UI is a collection of primitive and composable components built with React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, and Base UI. Copy, paste, and customize.

## What is Cubby UI?

Cubby UI is a collection of opinionated components built on [Base UI](https://base-ui.com) with React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS 4. It adds styling and functionality defaults on top of Base UI's unstyled, accessible primitives.

## Why Cubby UI?

- **Opinionated styling** - Pre-styled components built on Base UI's unstyled, accessible primitives. No need to design from scratch.
- **Common patterns built-in** - Abstracts common use cases so you don't have to wire up the same functionality repeatedly.
- **Full ownership** - Components are copied into your project via the [shadcn registry](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/registry), not imported from a package. Customize freely.

## Primitives and Composables

The component library is split into two groups, labelled on every component page and grouped in the sidebar:

- **Primitives** - A styled wrapper around a single Base UI primitive. [Button](/docs/components/button), [Dialog](/docs/components/dialog), and [Select](/docs/components/select) take an unstyled, accessible primitive and add Cubby UI's defaults. If Base UI ships it, you'll find the styled version here.
- **Composables** - A higher-level pattern composed from primitives, or an original component with no Base UI counterpart. [Command](/docs/components/command) builds a command menu on top of Dialog; [Circular Slider](/docs/components/circular-slider) is built from scratch. Composables list what they're **built on** so you can trace them back to their foundation.

## Other Options

There are several great UI libraries built on Base UI. Here are some worth checking out:

- [Shadcn/UI](https://ui.shadcn.com/create) - Shadcn/UI now offers all their ui components with Base UI as the component library. This is a great option if you are already using Shadcn/UI and want to use Base UI components.
- [Coss UI](https://coss.com/ui/docs) - Great collection of components built by the team of Cal.com that is also built on top of Base UI.

If you're looking for chart components, check out [Evil Charts](https://evilcharts.com/).

## Getting Started

Ready to start building? Head to the [Installation](/docs/getting-started/installation) guide to add Cubby UI to your project.

---

# surfaces.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joncoronel/cubby-ui/blob/main/content/docs/getting-started/surfaces.mdx

title: Surfaces
description: How Cubby keeps floating UI (popovers, dropdowns, dialogs, sheets) clearly lifted above whatever is behind it, at any nesting depth, in light and dark mode.

Open a dropdown and it should read as floating above the page. Open a popover _inside_ a dialog and it should still read as floating above the dialog. Surfaces is the system that makes that happen automatically, at any depth. Most of the time you never touch it.

## How elevation works

Every floating component (Popover, Dropdown, Dialog, Sheet, Drawer, and the rest) sits on a **level** from 1 to 8. The deeper something is nested, the higher its level. A card sits low, a dialog higher, a popover opened inside that dialog higher still. Each step up gets a lighter surface and a stronger shadow, so every layer reads as lifted above the one behind it.

<SurfaceNestingDemo />

There are eight levels because a nested case can go surprisingly deep, and the ladder should never run out. Most apps only ever reach for three or four.

One thing is worth knowing up front, because light and dark behave differently:

- **Light mode** keeps levels 3 and up pure white. The shadow alone does the lifting.
- **Dark mode** brightens the surface at each level, from `oklch(0.205)` at level 1 to `oklch(0.402)` at level 8, so each layer is visibly lighter than the one below.

## The two knobs

Every elevated component takes two props:

- `level` picks the **surface color**: which rung of the 1 to 8 ladder it sits on.
- `shadowLevel` picks the **shadow weight**: how heavily it casts.

They move independently. A wide dialog can sit on a mid surface but throw a heavy shadow; a small popover can sit higher yet cast a lighter one. Drag both and watch what changes:

<SurfacePlayground />

In light mode the surface stops changing above level 3 (they are all white) while the shadow keeps growing. In dark mode the surface color climbs with every level. That split is the whole idea: light mode leans on shadow, dark mode leans on color. Toggle the site theme to compare.

## Using it

Here is the part that matters most: **you rarely set either prop.** The defaults are tuned for the common case. A popover already sits at the right level; a dialog already sits higher.

The one time you reach for `level` is when you nest deeper than usual, like opening a popover from inside a dialog:

```tsx
// Default popover: level and shadow are already set for you.
<Popover>
  <PopoverTrigger>Open</PopoverTrigger>
  <PopoverContent>Default popover</PopoverContent>
</Popover>

// Inside a Dialog (which sits at level 5), bump the inner popover up.
<Dialog>
  <DialogContent>
    <Popover>
      <PopoverTrigger>Open inside dialog</PopoverTrigger>
      <PopoverContent level={7}>Pops above the dialog</PopoverContent>
    </Popover>
  </DialogContent>
</Dialog>
```

Bump `level` (not `shadowLevel`) when you nest. `shadowLevel` stays pinned per component, so a popover keeps reading like a popover no matter how deep it goes.

> **That is the whole API for most people.** Everything below is reference: the raw tokens, four helpers for building your own surfaces, and the knobs for retuning the system. Skip it until you need it.

## Reference

### The ladder

Eight surface colors, drawn here in your current theme:

<SurfaceTokensDemo />

| Level       | Light            | Dark               | Typical use                              |
| ----------- | ---------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| `surface-1` | `oklch(0.97 0 0)` | `oklch(0.205 ◇ ◆)` | Page background                          |
| `surface-2` | `oklch(0.985 0 0)` | `oklch(0.235 ◇ ◆)` | Inline toolbars, menubars                |
| `surface-3` | `oklch(1 0 0)`    | `oklch(0.264 ◇ ◆)` | Cards, popovers, dropdowns, tooltips     |
| `surface-4` | `oklch(1 0 0)`    | `oklch(0.293 ◇ ◆)` | Tabs indicator, transitional             |
| `surface-5` | `oklch(1 0 0)`    | `oklch(0.321 ◇ ◆)` | Dialogs, sheets, drawers, sub-menus      |
| `surface-6` | `oklch(1 0 0)`    | `oklch(0.348 ◇ ◆)` | Transitional                             |
| `surface-7` | `oklch(1 0 0)`    | `oklch(0.375 ◇ ◆)` | Popovers nested inside dialogs           |
| `surface-8` | `oklch(1 0 0)`    | `oklch(0.402 ◇ ◆)` | Maximum elevation (rare)                 |

`◇` is `var(--neutral-chroma)` and `◆` is `var(--neutral-hue)`; both come from the [brand tint](#brand-tint).

The named tokens you use elsewhere alias onto the ladder, so tuning the ladder updates all of them:

```css
--background: var(--surface-1);
--card: var(--surface-3); /* Card and Popover share level 3 */
--popover: var(--surface-3);
--sidebar: var(--surface-1);
```

### Shadows

`shadowLevel` tracks the visual weight of the element, not its surface level. Pick it by size:

- Under ~400px wide: `3`
- ~400 to 800px: `5`
- Over ~800px or fullscreen: `7`
- Never let `shadowLevel` exceed `level` by more than 2.

| Shadow             | Drop layers        | Feel                                        |
| ------------------ | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| `shadow-surface-1` | 0 (just a 1px ring) | Barely there                                |
| `shadow-surface-2` | 1                  | Tooltip, quiet                              |
| `shadow-surface-3` | 2                  | **Dropdown, popover, card**                 |
| `shadow-surface-4` | 3                  | Toast, floating elements with no trigger    |
| `shadow-surface-5` | 4                  | **Dialog, sheet**                           |
| `shadow-surface-6` | 5                  | Transitional                                |
| `shadow-surface-7` | 6                  | Dramatic (hero modals)                      |
| `shadow-surface-8` | 7                  | Maximum gravity (rare)                      |

In dark mode the recipe also adds an inset highlight and ring, giving surfaces a lit-from-above edge. In light mode those insets are no-ops and the drop shadow does everything.

### Component defaults

You do not need these day to day; they are what each component already uses. Reach in only to match a custom element to a built-in one.

<Accordion>
  <AccordionItem value="defaults">
    <AccordionTrigger indicatorType="chevron">
      Default level and shadow for every component
    </AccordionTrigger>
    <AccordionContent>

| Component            | Default `level` | Default `shadowLevel`               |
| -------------------- | --------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Tooltip              | `2`             | `2`                                 |
| Card                 | `3`             | `1`                                 |
| Table                | `3`             | `1`                                 |
| DataTable            | `3`             | `1`                                 |
| Code block           | `3`             | `1`                                 |
| ComponentPreview     | `3`             | `1`                                 |
| Popover              | `3`             | `3`                                 |
| Dropdown menu        | `3`             | `3`                                 |
| Dropdown sub-menu    | `5`             | `3`                                 |
| Context menu         | `3`             | `3`                                 |
| Context sub-menu     | `5`             | `3`                                 |
| Menubar (the bar)    | `2`             | `2`                                 |
| Menubar dropdown     | `3`             | `3`                                 |
| Menubar sub-menu     | `5`             | `3`                                 |
| NavigationMenu (bar) | `2`             | `2`                                 |
| NavigationMenu popup | `3`             | `3`                                 |
| NavigationMenu sub   | `5`             | `5`                                 |
| Select               | `3`             | `3`                                 |
| Toast                | `3`             | `4` (heavier, floats unattached)    |
| Dialog               | `5`             | `5`                                 |
| Alert dialog         | `5`             | `5`                                 |
| Sheet                | `5`             | `5`                                 |
| Drawer               | `5`             | `5`                                 |
| Command              | `3`             | `3`                                 |
| Combobox             | `3`             | `3`                                 |
| Autocomplete         | `3`             | `3`                                 |

The flat-card family (Card, Table, DataTable, code block, ComponentPreview) all share `solidSurface(3, 1)`: a surface-3 background with a 1px rim and no drop shadow. They are embedded containers, not floating popups, so they read as lifted just enough to define an edge rather than casting a shadow over content.

    </AccordionContent>
  </AccordionItem>
</Accordion>

### State overlays

Hover and selected backgrounds are translucent overlays, so they lift whatever surface they sit on by a fixed perceptual step, whatever its level:

```css
/* light */
--surface-hover: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.06);
--surface-selected: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.1);

/* dark */
--surface-hover: oklch(1 0 0 / 0.06);
--surface-selected: oklch(1 0 0 / 0.1);
```

```tsx
<div className="bg-(--surface-hover)">Hovered row</div>
<div className="bg-(--surface-selected)">Active row</div>
```

Because they are overlays and not fixed colors, hover on a `surface-3` row brightens by the same amount as on a `surface-7` row. Hover always reads as hover, even deeply nested. The values (6% for hover, 10% for selected) are matched to fluid-functionalism.

## Building your own surface

Making a custom floating container? Four helpers in `@/registry/default/lib/elevated` return Tailwind class strings. Drop them on any element you want elevated. Pick by situation:

| Helper            | When                                                                 |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `solidSurface`    | Most cases. The default choice.                                      |
| `elevatedSurface` | Sticky or opaque children sit near the edges (labels, inset footers). |
| `surfaceClasses`  | The surface already defines its own edge (a real CSS border).        |
| `flushSurface`    | A sheet or drawer pinned against a screen edge.                      |

### solidSurface(level, shadowLevel?)

Returns `bg-surface-N`, the combined drop and rim shadow, and exposes `--popup-surface` for descendants. Use it for any floating container without sticky or opaque children near its edges.

```tsx
import { solidSurface } from "@/registry/default/lib/elevated";

function Card({ children }) {
  return <div className={solidSurface(3)}>{children}</div>;
}
```

### elevatedSurface(level, shadowLevel?)

Same look as `solidSurface`, but it paints the rim on an `::after` layer above the content instead of in the box-shadow. Reach for it when sticky or opaque children sit near the edges: with `solidSurface` the rim lives in the box-shadow, so an opaque child at an edge renders on top and hides it. The two common cases are sticky group labels (Select, Combobox, Autocomplete) and opaque inset footers (Dialog, Sheet, Drawer, where a `bg-muted` footer would cover the bottom rim).

```tsx
import { elevatedSurface } from "@/registry/default/lib/elevated";

function MenuWithStickyHeader({ children }) {
  return (
    <div className={`relative overflow-clip rounded-xl ${elevatedSurface(3)}`}>
      <div className="sticky top-0 bg-(--popup-surface)">Sticky header</div>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}
```

The host must be positioned and have a border-radius so the rim clips correctly.

### surfaceClasses(level, shadowLevel?)

The primitive the others build on: just `bg-surface-N` and the downward drop shadow, no rim. Reach for it directly when the surface defines its own edge some other way (a real CSS border, a single-edge rim).

```tsx
import { surfaceClasses } from "@/registry/default/lib/elevated";

function PlainSurface({ children }) {
  return <div className={surfaceClasses(3)}>{children}</div>;
}
```

### flushSurface(level, innerEdge)

For viewport-flush containers: the `default` Sheet and Drawer variants that slide in pinned against a screen edge. Three of their four edges sit at the viewport boundary, so `solidSurface`'s always-downward shadow and four-edge rim point the wrong way. `flushSurface` instead casts the drop shadow toward the inner, content-facing edge, and paints a single-edge rim on that same edge. Pass the content-facing edge directly, or derive it from the attach side with `INNER_EDGE_FROM_ATTACH_SIDE` (`right → left`, `bottom → top`, and so on).

```tsx
import {
  flushSurface,
  INNER_EDGE_FROM_ATTACH_SIDE,
} from "@/registry/default/lib/elevated";

// Right-flush sheet: shadow and rim on the left (inner) edge.
function RightSheet({ children }) {
  return (
    <div className={`fixed inset-y-0 right-0 ${flushSurface(5, "left")}`}>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

// Or derive the edge from the attach side:
// flushSurface(5, INNER_EDGE_FROM_ATTACH_SIDE[side])
```

## Customizing the system

### Brand tint

Two variables at the top of `:root` tint every neutral in the system, so you can retune the whole thing from one place:

```css
--neutral-hue: 275; /* hue angle 0–360. Cool purple-blue. */
--neutral-chroma: 0.004; /* tint strength for mid-tone neutrals */
--neutral-chroma-low: 0.002; /* tint strength near the lightness extremes */
```

Change `--neutral-hue` to rotate the entire palette without touching individual tokens:

- `0 to 90`: warm (red, orange, amber, yellow). Try ~70 for amber.
- `90 to 180`: green.
- `180 to 270`: cool (cyan, blue). The primary lives at 250.
- `270 to 330`: cool purple and violet. The neutral tint sits at 275.
- `330 to 360`: pink and magenta, heading back toward warm.

`--neutral-chroma` around `0.005 to 0.01` is the visibility floor; we sit just under at `0.004` for a quieter feel.

### Tracking the level from descendants

When you set `level`, the helpers expose `--popup-surface` on that element. Children can match the surface color without hardcoding a level:

```tsx
// Arrow that matches whatever level the popup is at.
<svg className="fill-(--popup-surface,var(--popover))" />

// Sticky label inside a Select that blends with the popup.
<div className="sticky top-0 bg-(--popup-surface)">Group label</div>
```

The `var(--popover)` fallback keeps things working if the variable is not set in some context.

## Design decisions

Surfaces is inspired by [fluidfunctionalism.com/elevated](https://www.fluidfunctionalism.com/elevated), adapted to a prop-based API instead of a context, with a few deliberate divergences from a strict "tint everything on the ladder" reading.

<Accordion multiple>
  <AccordionItem value="pure-neutral">
    <AccordionTrigger indicatorType="chevron">
      Light surfaces are pure neutral
    </AccordionTrigger>
    <AccordionContent>

Every light-mode background (the surface ladder, `--muted`, `--secondary`, `--accent`, `--input`, sidebar surfaces) has chroma 0: literally neutral gray and white. The brand tint applies only to text foregrounds in light mode and to every dark-mode surface and token.

Net effect: light mode reads as a clean canvas, dark mode carries the brand identity. It is a common pattern (Linear, Vercel, Stripe): tint on a near-white page reads as a wash rather than a signature, while in dark mode the same chroma has room to express.

    </AccordionContent>
  </AccordionItem>
  <AccordionItem value="muted">
    <AccordionTrigger indicatorType="chevron">
      `--muted` lives off the ladder
    </AccordionTrigger>
    <AccordionContent>

`--muted` is a standalone token (`oklch(0.94 0 0)` light, `oklch(0.24 ◇ ◆)` dark), not aliased to a surface level. The ladder represents _lifted_ surfaces (up from the page); `--muted` represents the _recessed_ category: inset wells, code blocks, command-palette wells, quiet differentiation strips.

The reference aliases `--muted` to `surface-2` because its system has no recessed concept. Cubby does, so `--muted` stays separate.

    </AccordionContent>
  </AccordionItem>
  <AccordionItem value="form-fields">
    <AccordionTrigger indicatorType="chevron">
      Form fields use `--input` and `--input-elevated`
    </AccordionTrigger>
    <AccordionContent>

Form fields come in two appearances, exposed as a `variant` prop on Input, Textarea, NumberField, InputGroup, OTP, Combobox, Autocomplete, Checkbox, and Radio:

```tsx
// Default: opaque "clean lifted card" look. Use on the page.
<Input />

// Elevated: translucent overlay that adapts to its substrate. Use inside a
// Card, Dialog, or popover, where the opaque default would disappear.
<Card>
  <Input variant="elevated" />
</Card>
```

`--input` resolves to `var(--surface-3)` in both modes (white in light, surface-3 in dark). `--input-elevated` is the same family as the state overlays but stronger, so it adapts to any substrate:

```css
/* light */
--input: var(--surface-3); /* opaque, "clean lifted" */
--input-elevated: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.08); /* 8% black overlay */

/* dark */
--input-elevated: oklch(1 0 0 / 0.09); /* 9% white overlay */
```

One token cannot satisfy every context: an opaque white input feels right on the page, but disappears on a Card or inside a Dialog (also white in light mode), where the translucent overlay is needed instead. The `variant` prop lets the caller choose per context.

Switch skips the variant. Its unchecked track has to contrast with both its thumb and the parent surface at once, and a single translucent `bg-input-elevated` overlay handles both: it adapts to whatever it sits on while staying a clear gray against the thumb. So Switch has no `variant` prop; it always uses `bg-input-elevated`.

    </AccordionContent>
  </AccordionItem>
  <AccordionItem value="overlays">
    <AccordionTrigger indicatorType="chevron">
      Pure black and white overlays stay untinted
    </AccordionTrigger>
    <AccordionContent>

`--border`, `--surface-hover`, `--surface-selected`, the dark-mode shadow ring values, `--surface-shadow-*`, and the rest use literal `oklch(0 0 0)` or `oklch(1 0 0)` rather than tinted near-black or near-white. At translucent alpha they borrow their visible color from the tinted substrate beneath, so tinting the overlay itself contributes almost nothing while making the CSS harder to read.

    </AccordionContent>
  </AccordionItem>
  <AccordionItem value="asymmetric">
    <AccordionTrigger indicatorType="chevron">
      Inset patterns are mode-asymmetric
    </AccordionTrigger>
    <AccordionContent>

The Command well uses `bg-surface-3 dark:bg-surface-1`. In light mode that is a lifted white card inside a gray strip; in dark mode it is a cutout to the page color. Each mode gets strong contrast its own way. A symmetric version (one token for both modes) has a weak mode by construction.

    </AccordionContent>
  </AccordionItem>
</Accordion>

## Token reference

Every token lives on `:root` and is exposed as a Tailwind utility through `@theme inline`. Tune any of them in your `globals.css` to customize the system without touching the components.

```css
/* Substrate */
--surface-1 .. --surface-8       /* surface colors */
--surface-shadow-1 .. -8         /* drop-shadow recipes → shadow-surface-N */
--surface-rim-1 .. -8            /* inset rim recipes → shadow-surface-rim-N */

/* State */
--surface-hover                  /* +6% perceived brightness overlay */
--surface-selected               /* +10% perceived brightness overlay */
--input                          /* opaque form-field bg = surface-3 */
--input-elevated                 /* stronger overlay for elevated fields and Switch */
--surface-rim-color              /* single-edge rim color (flush sheets) */
--popup-surface                  /* set by the helpers, read by descendants */

/* Tint controls */
--neutral-hue                    /* one knob: rotates the whole tint */
--neutral-chroma                 /* tint strength for mid-tone neutrals */
--neutral-chroma-low             /* tint strength near the gamut extremes */

/* Aliases */
--background  →  var(--surface-1)
--card        →  var(--surface-3)
--popover     →  var(--surface-3)
--sidebar     →  var(--surface-1)
```

# theming.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joncoronel/cubby-ui/blob/main/content/docs/getting-started/theming.mdx

title: Theming
description: A guide to styling components with our color system.

## Overview

Our styling system builds upon [shadcn/ui's CSS variables approach](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/theming) with additional status colors and design tokens.

## Installation

<Tabs defaultValue="manual">

<TabsList>
  <TabsTrigger value="cli">CLI</TabsTrigger>
  <TabsTrigger value="manual">Manual</TabsTrigger>
</TabsList>

<TabsPanels>
<TabsContent value="cli">

For an existing shadcn project, add the theme:

<PackageManagerCommand command="shadcn@latest add @cubby-ui/style" />

Starting a new project? Scaffold shadcn and install the theme in one command:

<PackageManagerCommand command="shadcn@latest init @cubby-ui/style" />

This adds the theme CSS variables to your project. See [Installation](/docs/getting-started/installation) for the full setup.

</TabsContent>

<TabsContent value="manual">

Copy and paste the following into your `globals.css` file:

```css title="globals.css"
:root {
  --radius: 0.75rem;

  /* Brand-hue tint controls — change these to retune the entire
     neutral palette. */
  --neutral-hue: 270;
  --neutral-chroma: 0.004;
  --neutral-chroma-low: 0.002;

  /* Background colors — aliased to the surface ladder */
  --background: var(--surface-1);
  --foreground: oklch(0.18 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --card: var(--surface-3);
  --card-foreground: var(--foreground);
  --popover: var(--surface-3);
  --popover-foreground: var(--foreground);

  /* Primary & accent colors */
  --primary: oklch(0.6 0.2 250);
  --primary-foreground: oklch(1 0 0);
  /* Primary as text on a neutral plate (primary-soft button); derived from
     --primary so it tracks any brand color. Brightened in dark below. */
  --primary-soft-foreground: var(--primary);
  /* Destructive as text on a tinted plate (destructive-soft button); derived */
  --destructive-soft-foreground: var(--destructive);
  --neutral: oklch(0.22 0 0);
  --neutral-foreground: oklch(
    0.98 var(--neutral-chroma-low) var(--neutral-hue)
  );
  --secondary: oklch(0.92 0 0);
  --secondary-foreground: oklch(0.32 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --muted: oklch(0.94 0 0);
  --muted-foreground: oklch(0.5 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --accent: oklch(0.91 0 0);
  --accent-foreground: oklch(0.22 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --destructive: oklch(0.53 0.19 25);
  --destructive-foreground: oklch(
    0.98 var(--neutral-chroma-low) var(--neutral-hue)
  );

  /* Hover-state colors — mix direction chosen per-token to shift away
     from each token's natural lightness, so the change is always visible.
     --neutral is already dark (0.22) so it lightens instead of darkens. */
  --primary-hover: color-mix(in oklch, var(--primary), black 5%);
  --neutral-hover: color-mix(in oklch, var(--neutral), white 10%);
  --destructive-hover: color-mix(in oklch, var(--destructive), black 5%);
  --secondary-hover: color-mix(in oklch, var(--secondary), black 5%);
  --outline-hover: color-mix(in oklch, var(--card), black 5%);

  /* Borders & form fields */
  --border: oklch(0 0 0 / 10%);
  --input: var(--surface-3);
  --input-elevated: oklch(0 0 0 / 8%);
  --ring: oklch(0.55 0.2 250);
  --scrollbar: oklch(0.87 0 0);

  /* Sidebar colors — aliased to the core tokens so the sidebar palette tracks
     the rest of the system. No `.dark` overrides needed except --sidebar-border
     (the aliases resolve per mode). */
  --sidebar: var(--surface-1);
  --sidebar-foreground: var(--foreground);
  --sidebar-primary: var(--primary);
  --sidebar-primary-foreground: var(--primary-foreground);
  --sidebar-accent: var(--accent);
  --sidebar-accent-foreground: var(--accent-foreground);
  /* Opaque equivalent of --border for the resize rail's solid bg. */
  --sidebar-border: oklch(0.9 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --sidebar-ring: var(--ring);

  /* Status colors */
  --danger: oklch(0.97 0.04 25);
  --danger-foreground: oklch(0.55 0.18 25);
  --danger-border: oklch(0.9 0.1 25);
  --warning: oklch(0.98 0.06 85);
  --warning-foreground: oklch(0.58 0.14 85);
  --warning-border: oklch(0.92 0.1 85);
  --info: oklch(0.97 0.04 250);
  --info-foreground: oklch(0.45 0.2 250);
  --info-border: oklch(0.9 0.1 250);
  --success: oklch(0.97 0.04 145);
  --success-foreground: oklch(0.48 0.18 145);
  --success-border: oklch(0.9 0.1 145);

  /* Surface elevation ladder (1-8) — light surfaces stay neutral.
     Shadow alone carries elevation here. */
  --surface-1: oklch(0.97 0 0);
  --surface-2: oklch(0.985 0 0);
  --surface-3: oklch(1 0 0);
  --surface-4: oklch(1 0 0);
  --surface-5: oklch(1 0 0);
  --surface-6: oklch(1 0 0);
  --surface-7: oklch(1 0 0);
  --surface-8: oklch(1 0 0);

  /* State overlays */
  --surface-hover: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.06);
  --surface-selected: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.1);
  --surface-rim-color: oklch(0 0 0 / 0);

  /* Light shadow recipe — opacity decreases with blur radius for
     natural light fall-off. */
  --surface-shadow-ring: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.06);
  --surface-shadow-near: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.06);
  --surface-shadow-mid: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.05);
  --surface-shadow-far: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.04);
  --surface-shadow-ambient: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.03);
  --surface-shadow-1: 0 0 0 1px var(--surface-shadow-ring);
  --surface-shadow-2:
    0 0 0 1px var(--surface-shadow-ring),
    0 1px 1px -0.5px var(--surface-shadow-near);
  --surface-shadow-3:
    0 0 0 1px var(--surface-shadow-ring),
    0 1px 1px -0.5px var(--surface-shadow-near),
    0 3px 3px -1.5px var(--surface-shadow-mid);
  --surface-shadow-4:
    0 0 0 1px var(--surface-shadow-ring),
    0 1px 1px -0.5px var(--surface-shadow-near),
    0 3px 3px -1.5px var(--surface-shadow-mid),
    0 6px 6px -3px var(--surface-shadow-mid);
  --surface-shadow-5:
    0 0 0 1px var(--surface-shadow-ring),
    0 1px 1px -0.5px var(--surface-shadow-near),
    0 3px 3px -1.5px var(--surface-shadow-mid),
    0 6px 6px -3px var(--surface-shadow-mid),
    0 12px 12px -6px var(--surface-shadow-far);
  --surface-shadow-6:
    0 0 0 1px var(--surface-shadow-ring),
    0 1px 1px -0.5px var(--surface-shadow-near),
    0 3px 3px -1.5px var(--surface-shadow-mid),
    0 6px 6px -3px var(--surface-shadow-mid),
    0 12px 12px -6px var(--surface-shadow-far),
    0 24px 24px -12px var(--surface-shadow-far);
  --surface-shadow-7:
    0 0 0 1px var(--surface-shadow-ring),
    0 1px 1px -0.5px var(--surface-shadow-near),
    0 3px 3px -1.5px var(--surface-shadow-mid),
    0 6px 6px -3px var(--surface-shadow-mid),
    0 12px 12px -6px var(--surface-shadow-far),
    0 24px 24px -12px var(--surface-shadow-far),
    0 48px 48px -24px var(--surface-shadow-ambient);
  --surface-shadow-8:
    0 0 0 1px var(--surface-shadow-ring),
    0 1px 1px -0.5px var(--surface-shadow-near),
    0 3px 3px -1.5px var(--surface-shadow-mid),
    0 6px 6px -3px var(--surface-shadow-mid),
    0 12px 12px -6px var(--surface-shadow-far),
    0 24px 24px -12px var(--surface-shadow-far),
    0 48px 48px -24px var(--surface-shadow-ambient),
    0 96px 96px -48px var(--surface-shadow-ambient);

  /* Rim overlay — no-op in light mode */
  --surface-rim-1: 0 0 transparent;
  --surface-rim-2: 0 0 transparent;
  --surface-rim-3: 0 0 transparent;
  --surface-rim-4: 0 0 transparent;
  --surface-rim-5: 0 0 transparent;
  --surface-rim-6: 0 0 transparent;
  --surface-rim-7: 0 0 transparent;
  --surface-rim-8: 0 0 transparent;
}

.dark {

  --neutral: oklch(0.95 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --neutral-foreground: oklch(0.13 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));

  --secondary-foreground: oklch(0.94 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --muted: oklch(0.24 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --muted-foreground: oklch(0.73 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --accent: oklch(0.31 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --accent-foreground: oklch(0.95 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --destructive: oklch(0.5 0.22 25);
  --destructive-foreground: oklch(1 0 0);
  /* Brighten --primary toward white so primary-soft stays readable on the
     darker secondary plate. Derived, so it tracks the consumer's brand color. */
  --primary-soft-foreground: color-mix(in oklch, var(--primary), white 30%);
  /* Same treatment for destructive-soft's label on its tinted plate. */
  --destructive-soft-foreground: color-mix(in oklch, var(--destructive), white 30%);

     in dark (0.95) so it darkens instead of brightens. */

  --neutral-hover: color-mix(in oklch, var(--neutral), black 10%);
  --destructive-hover: color-mix(in oklch, var(--destructive), white 15%);

  --border: oklch(1 0 0 / 10%);

  --info-border: oklch(0.36 0.11 250);
  --success: oklch(0.26 0.07 145);
  --success-foreground: oklch(0.72 0.15 145);
  --success-border: oklch(0.36 0.11 145);

  /* Dark surface ladder */
  --surface-1: oklch(0.205 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --surface-2: oklch(0.235 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));
  --surface-3: oklch(0.264 var(--neutral-chroma) var(--neutral-hue));

  --surface-hover: oklch(1 0 0 / 0.06);
  --surface-selected: oklch(1 0 0 / 0.1);
  --surface-rim-color: oklch(1 0 0 / 0.04);

  /* Dark-only tokens for the rim recipe */

  --surface-shadow-near: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.18);

  --surface-shadow-far: oklch(0 0 0 / 0.14);

  --surface-shadow-4:
    0 0 0 1px oklch(0 0 0 / 0.14), 0 1px 1px -0.5px var(--surface-shadow-near),
    0 3px 3px -1.5px var(--surface-shadow-mid),
    0 6px 6px -3px var(--surface-shadow-mid);
  --surface-shadow-5:
```
